unit.title: When the rules you trusted are broken
unit.needIt: People can survive danger. What breaks them is betrayal by those in charge of what is right. That is true in war, at work and in families.
unit.why: The lecture looks at how people react when the rules of the world break down. It uses stories from ancient wars and modern conflicts to show how losing trust in 'the right way' of doing things can leave deep scars on the human soul.
unit.outcome: Understand how a loss of social order leads to moral injury and personal trauma.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you feel unsafe in a crowd or when you find it hard to trust a stranger. It also shows up when you feel angry because someone broke a fair rule in your workplace or school.
unit.do: Think of a time you felt a loss of trust. Write down one small way you can rebuild a sense of order in your own daily routine.

quiz.q: What is the special function of a human being according to Aristotle?
quiz.why: Aristotle says the human good is the expression of reason.
quiz.quote: And the special function of a human being, says Aristotle, is the expression of reason, the soul's activity that expresses reason, in one of the standard translations.

quiz.q: What is the special function of a human being?
quiz.why: Aristotle says the human good is the expression of reason.
quiz.quote: So the human good on the Aristotelian picture has got to be the thing about human beings that sets them apart from other sorts of creatures.

quiz.why: Virtue is when your instinctive responses match your reflective commitments.
quiz.quote: So virtue on Aristotle's picture is being such that instinctive responses fall into line with your reflective commitments.

quiz.q: What is a virtue of thought?
quiz.why: Virtues of thought are things like knowing facts that are taught.
quiz.quote: It's a virtue of thought to know facts about the periodic table, or to know information of a particular kind about the political structures around you.

quiz.q: How are virtues of character acquired?
quiz.why: Character virtues are built through repeated actions over time.
quiz.quote: They are things that you process in the spirited and appetitive parts of your soul as the result of a kind of cultivation of habit.

quiz.q: How are virtues of character acquired?
quiz.why: Virtues of character are completed in us through habit.
quiz.quote: They are things for which we have the capacity, and they are completed in us through habit.

quiz.q: What happens when you practice a skill like playing the piano?
choices: You do it until it is instinctive
quiz.why: Aristotle says we learn to be something by acting like that was what we already were.
quiz.quote: The way that we cultivate habits is first by consciously structuring our lives in such a way that the habit that we wish to cultivate becomes part of our behavioral repertoire.

crystal.key: Virtue is the harmony of the soul through practiced habits.

decoys.text: Virtue is something you are born with.
decoys.why: Aristotle says virtues of character are not by nature.

decoys.text: Moral injury is only a physical wound.
decoys.why: The lecture says moral injuries are not physical injuries.

crystal.aha: When we practice habits that align our instincts with our reason, we create a harmonious soul that can withstand the disorder of the world.
